sections.name: Rendering and presentation
sections.note: What a renderer actually draws - width, direction, orientation, and whether an emoji font will claim the character out from under the one you chose.

sections.name: Breaking and segmentation
sections.note: Where the text may come apart around it: line wrapping, grapheme clusters, word and sentence boundaries. A marker that takes a break opportunity its neighbours do not will not hold a column.

sections.name: Vintage
sections.note: How long a codepoint has existed. The strongest single predictor of whether a font will have it at all - which is a different question from how it is treated.

sections.name: Script
sections.note: Which writing system a glyph belongs to, and how widely that system is used. Bears on font selection rather than on renderer behaviour.

sections.name: Classification
sections.note: What kind of character it is, in the Unicode Character Database's own terms.

sections.name: Normalisation
sections.note: Whether the codepoint survives normalisation unchanged. An NFKC-unstable glyph may not come back the same from a round trip through other software.

sections.name: Identifier and case
sections.note: Whether the codepoint may appear in a programming identifier, and how it cases.

sections.name: Other binary properties
sections.note: Everything else the UCD marks as a yes/no property of a codepoint.

props.name: Age
props.gloss: The Unicode version in which this codepoint was assigned a character.
props.note: Filtered as 'not after', because that is the direction that matters: a font built in 2012 cannot contain a character added in 2020. Age is the single strongest predictor of whether a glyph will be present at all, which makes it the first filter to reach for when hunting something that renders consistently. It says nothing about whether a font that could have the glyph does have it.

props.name: Script
props.gloss: The writing system the codepoint belongs to, as an ISO 15924 script code.
props.note: Grouped by the UAX #31 identifier usage that CLDR publishes in scriptMetadata.txt, rather than by a grouping invented here. That published classification is what 'common, rare, ancient' actually resolves to. Four cells in five on this page are Common - they belong to no single script - so the grouping exists mainly to make the remaining fifth navigable.

groups.label: Common - no single script
groups.note: Common. Belongs to no one script: the punctuation, symbols, digits and marks shared across writing systems. Most of this page.

groups.label: Widely used modern scripts
groups.note: Widely used modern scripts. UAX #31 recommends them for identifiers, and font coverage is correspondingly broad.

groups.label: Limited modern use
groups.note: In modern use, but by small communities. Coverage outside specialist fonts is patchy.

groups.label: Historic and obsolete scripts
groups.note: Historic and obsolete scripts, kept for scholarly use. UAX #31 excludes them from identifiers; expect coverage only in dedicated fonts.

props.scx_note: Script_Extensions widens the match to every script a character is used in rather than the one it is filed under. It differs from Script for 280 cells here.

props.name: General_Category
props.gloss: General_Category - the broadest classification the UCD makes of a codepoint.
props.note: Two letters: the first is the major class (Letter, Mark, Number, Punctuation, Symbol, Separator, Other), the second the subclass. Every codepoint has exactly one.

values.label: Lowercase_Letter
values.note: Lowercase letter.

values.label: Modifier_Letter
values.note: Modifier letter - a letter-like character that modifies the one before it, such as a raised ring or a tone letter.

values.label: Uppercase_Letter
values.note: Uppercase letter.

values.label: Decimal_Number
values.note: Decimal digit - a digit that takes part in ordinary positional notation.

values.label: Letter_Number
values.note: Letter-like number, such as a Roman numeral or a counting rod.

values.label: Other_Number
values.note: Other number - fractions, circled and superscript digits, numerals that are not decimal digits.

values.label: Connector_Punctuation
values.note: Connector punctuation - joins other characters, such as the low line.

values.label: Dash_Punctuation
values.note: Dash punctuation - hyphens and dashes of every length.

values.label: Close_Punctuation
values.note: Closing bracket of a pair.

values.label: Final_Punctuation
values.note: Final quotation mark - the closing half of a directional quote pair.

values.label: Initial_Punctuation
values.note: Initial quotation mark - the opening half of a directional quote pair.

values.label: Other_Punctuation
values.note: Other punctuation - everything punctuation-like that is not a bracket, dash or quote.

values.label: Open_Punctuation
values.note: Opening bracket of a pair.

values.label: Currency_Symbol
values.note: Currency symbol.

values.label: Modifier_Symbol
values.note: Modifier symbol - a free-standing accent or similar, spacing rather than combining.

values.label: Math_Symbol
values.note: Mathematical symbol - operators, relations, arrows used mathematically.

values.label: Other_Symbol
values.note: Other symbol - the large residual class holding most pictographs, geometric shapes and dingbats.

props.name: East_Asian_Width
props.gloss: East_Asian_Width - how much horizontal room a codepoint is expected to take in a legacy East Asian context.
props.note: The only width Unicode itself specifies. Advance width lives in the font, not in the UCD, so this is the property a terminal uses to decide how many cells a glyph occupies - and the one that has to be uniform across a candidate set if a marker is to hold its column. Ambiguous is the trap: its width depends on the context the terminal thinks it is in, so the same glyph occupies one cell for one user and two for another.

values.label: Ambiguous
values.note: Ambiguous. One cell or two depending on context and terminal configuration. The value most likely to break a column.

values.label: Fullwidth
values.note: Fullwidth. Two cells; a compatibility variant of a narrow character.

values.label: Halfwidth
values.note: Halfwidth. One cell; a compatibility variant of a wide character.

values.label: Neutral
values.note: Neutral. Not used in legacy East Asian encodings; conventionally one cell.

values.label: Narrow
values.note: Narrow. One cell, with an explicit wide counterpart elsewhere.

values.label: Wide
values.note: Wide. Two cells.

props.name: Bidi_Class
props.gloss: Bidi_Class - the role this codepoint plays in the bidirectional algorithm.
props.note: Determines how the character reorders when mixed with right-to-left text. A neutral character between two runs takes its direction from its surroundings, which is a way a marker glyph can move without the font changing.

values.label: Arabic_Letter
values.note: Arabic letter. Strongly right-to-left.

values.label: Arabic_Number
values.note: Arabic-Indic number.

values.label: Common_Separator
values.note: Common number separator, such as the comma and full stop between digits.

values.label: European_Number
values.note: European number - ordinary digits.

values.label: European_Separator
values.note: European number separator - plus and minus between digits.

values.label: European_Terminator
values.note: European number terminator - currency signs, per cent, degree.

values.label: Left_To_Right
values.note: Strongly left-to-right.

values.label: Other_Neutral
values.note: Other neutral. Takes direction from its surroundings. Most symbols and punctuation are here.

values.label: Right_To_Left
values.note: Strongly right-to-left, other than Arabic.

props.name: Line_Break
props.gloss: Line_Break - how a line-breaking algorithm may break around this codepoint.
props.note: Deferred earlier in this project as too complex for a table column; offered here as a filter because the value set turned out to be one of the better-spread on the page. It describes where text may wrap, not how the glyph is drawn.

values.label: Ambiguous
values.note: Ambiguous - alphabetic or ideographic depending on context.

values.label: Alphabetic
values.note: Ordinary alphabetic character. The default for most symbols here.

values.label: Break_Both
values.note: May break either side, and binds the two lines together - the em dash.

values.label: Break_After
values.note: May break after.

values.label: Break_Before
values.note: May break before.

values.label: Contingent_Break
values.note: Contingent break - the surrounding context decides, as for an inline object.

values.label: Close_Punctuation
values.note: Closing punctuation; no break before it.

values.label: Close_Parenthesis
values.note: Closing parenthesis, treated slightly differently from other closers.

values.label: E_Base
values.note: Emoji base - may take a skin-tone modifier.

values.label: Exclamation
values.note: Exclamation or question mark; no break before.

values.label: Glue
values.note: Non-breaking glue - forbids a break on either side.

values.label: Hyphen
values.note: The hyphen-minus specifically.

values.label: Ideographic
values.note: Ideographic. May break on either side, which is how CJK text wraps.

values.label: Inseparable
values.note: Inseparable - a run such as an ellipsis that must not be split.

values.label: Infix_Numeric
values.note: Infix numeric separator, such as the colon or comma inside a number.

values.label: Nonstarter
values.note: Non-starter - may not begin a line.

values.label: Numeric
values.note: Numeric.

values.label: Open_Punctuation
values.note: Opening punctuation; no break after it.

values.label: Postfix_Numeric
values.note: Postfix numeric, such as a per-cent sign after a number.

values.label: Prefix_Numeric
values.note: Prefix numeric, such as a currency sign before a number.

values.label: Quotation
values.note: Quotation mark, ambiguous as to which end it is.

values.label: Regional_Indicator
values.note: Regional indicator - the letters that pair into flags.

values.label: Complex_Context
values.note: Complex context - a South East Asian script needing dictionary line-breaking.

values.label: Break_Symbols
values.note: Symbol allowing a break after, chiefly the solidus.

props.name: Bidi_Paired_Bracket_Type
props.gloss: Bidi_Paired_Bracket_Type - whether this codepoint is one half of a bracket pair the bidi algorithm should keep matched.
props.note: Deferred earlier in this project alongside Line_Break, and offered here on the same reasoning. A narrow property: only 118 cells on this page are either half of a pair. The partner codepoint itself is a mapping rather than a class, so it is not filterable and appears in the info box instead.

values.label: Close
values.note: Closing half of a bidi bracket pair.

values.label: None
values.note: Not a paired bracket.

values.label: Open
values.note: Opening half of a bidi bracket pair.

props.name: Vertical_Orientation
props.gloss: Vertical_Orientation - how the glyph is oriented when the text is set vertically.
props.note: UAX #50. Only bites in vertical CJK layout, but it is not marginal on this inventory: 1,922 cells are upright against 2,771 rotated. A candidate set mixing the two would look coherent horizontally and broken the moment it was set vertically, which is the kind of failure that only shows up in someone else's document.

values.label: Rotated
values.note: Rotated 90° clockwise in vertical text. The default for most characters.

values.label: Transformed_Rotated
values.note: Transformed to a rotated variant - a different glyph, then rotated.

values.label: Transformed_Upright
values.note: Transformed to an upright variant - a different glyph, not a rotation.

values.label: Upright
values.note: Upright. Drawn as-is in vertical text.

props.name: Decomposition_Type
props.gloss: Decomposition_Type - what kind of decomposition the codepoint has, if any.
props.note: More useful than the mapping itself, because the tag says why the character is unstable. Sup is what folds an ordinal away under NFKC; Enc and Sqr would fold an enclosed or squared shape; Wide and Nar are the fullwidth and halfwidth compatibility forms. Canonical decomposition is a different matter - it round-trips, so it is not a hazard in the same way.

values.label: Canonical
values.note: Canonically equivalent to a sequence. Round-trips under NFC, so not a compatibility hazard.

values.label: None
values.note: No decomposition. The codepoint stands on its own under every normalisation form.

values.label: Circle
values.note: An enclosed form - a character inside a circle.

values.label: Compat
values.note: A compatibility variant with no more specific tag.

values.label: Font
values.note: A font variant - the styled mathematical alphanumerics are here.

values.label: Fraction
values.note: A vulgar fraction.

values.label: Isolated
values.note: The isolated contextual form of an Arabic letter.

values.label: Narrow
values.note: A halfwidth compatibility variant.

values.label: Nobreak
values.note: A non-breaking variant of another character.

values.label: Small
values.note: A small form variant, from the CJK small-form block.

values.label: Square
values.note: A squared form, typically a CJK abbreviation set in one cell.

values.label: Super
values.note: A superscript form. This is what makes an ordinal fold away under NFKC.

values.label: Vertical
values.note: A glyph variant used in vertical text.

values.label: Wide
values.note: A fullwidth compatibility variant.

props.name: Canonical_Combining_Class
props.gloss: Canonical_Combining_Class - the reordering weight a combining mark carries during normalisation.
props.note: Zero for anything that is not a combining mark, which on this page is very nearly everything. Worth having as an assertion rather than a sift: a non-zero value would mean the character reorders under normalisation, which for a structural marker is disqualifying.

values.label: Not_Reordered
values.note: Not reordered. The character is not a combining mark, or is one that keeps its place.

props.inert: every cell on this page has the same value, 0

props.name: Numeric_Type
props.gloss: Numeric_Type - whether the codepoint has a numeric value, and of what kind.

values.label: Decimal
values.note: A digit usable in ordinary positional decimal notation.

values.label: Digit
values.note: Digit-like but not usable positionally - superscripts, circled digits.

values.label: None
values.note: No numeric value.

values.label: Numeric
values.note: Has a numeric value that is not a plain digit: fractions, Roman numerals, counting rods.

props.name: Identifier_Status
props.gloss: Identifier_Status - UTS #39's verdict on whether the codepoint is safe in a security-sensitive identifier.
props.note: Not a UCD property; it comes from Unicode's security mechanisms, vendored separately. Almost every symbol is Restricted, which is expected rather than alarming - these are not characters anyone should be writing identifiers with. Its use here is as a cross-check that a candidate is not secretly a letter.

values.label: Allowed
values.note: Permitted in identifiers under UTS #39.

values.label: Restricted
values.note: Not permitted. The reason is in Identifier_Type.

props.name: Identifier_Type
props.gloss: Identifier_Type - UTS #39's reason for a codepoint's identifier status. A codepoint may carry more than one.
props.note: The more interesting half of the pair, because the reasons are quiet warnings about a character's standing that no other property surfaces. Technical in particular flags characters that exist for legacy systems rather than for text. Set-valued, so the filter asks whether a codepoint carries a reason, not whether that is its only one.

values.label: Deprecated
values.note: Its use is discouraged by the standard.

values.label: Exclusion
values.note: From a historic or obsolete script.

values.label: Inclusion
values.note: Included by explicit exception.

values.label: Limited_Use
values.note: Used by a small community.

values.label: Not_NFKC
values.note: Excluded because it does not survive compatibility normalisation.

values.label: Not_XID
values.note: Simply not identifier-legal; the ordinary case for a symbol.

values.label: Obsolete
values.note: No longer in current use.

values.label: Recommended
values.note: Positively recommended for identifiers.

values.label: Technical
values.note: Exists for legacy or specialised technical use rather than for running text. Worth avoiding in a format meant to last.

values.label: Uncommon_Use
values.note: In use, but rarely.

props.name: Grapheme_Cluster_Break
props.gloss: Grapheme_Cluster_Break - the codepoint's role in finding user-perceived character boundaries.
props.note: Nearly constant across this page: 4,830 of 4,832 cells are Other. That is itself the finding - the inventory is almost entirely made of standalone characters that form a cluster on their own, which is what you would want of a marker.

values.label: Other
values.note: Forms a grapheme cluster on its own.

values.label: Regional_Indicator
values.note: One of the 26 letters that pair to make a flag; two of them join into one cluster.

props.name: Word_Break
props.gloss: Word_Break - the codepoint's role in finding word boundaries.
props.note: Decides where a double-click selects to, and where a word-wise cursor movement stops.

values.label: ALetter
values.note: Behaves as a letter for word-boundary purposes.

values.label: Double_Quote
values.note: The straight double quote, which has its own rule.

values.label: ExtendNumLet
values.note: Extends a word or number across itself, as the low line does.

values.label: Katakana
values.note: Katakana, which forms words without spaces.

values.label: MidLetter
values.note: May appear inside a word between letters, such as the apostrophe.

values.label: MidNum
values.note: May appear inside a number between digits, such as the comma.

values.label: MidNumLet
values.note: May appear inside either a word or a number, such as the full stop.

values.label: Numeric
values.note: Behaves as a digit for word-boundary purposes.

values.label: Other
values.note: Not part of a word; a boundary falls on both sides.

values.label: Regional_Indicator
values.note: One of the flag-forming letters.

values.label: Single_Quote
values.note: The straight single quote, which has its own rule.

props.name: Sentence_Break
props.gloss: Sentence_Break - the codepoint's role in finding sentence boundaries.

values.label: ATerm
values.note: Ambiguous terminator - the full stop, which may also be a decimal point or an abbreviation.

values.label: Close
values.note: A closing bracket or quote, which may follow a terminator before the sentence really ends.

values.label: Lower
values.note: Lowercase letter; its appearance after a full stop suggests the sentence did not end.

values.label: Numeric
values.note: A digit.

values.label: OLetter
values.note: A letter in a script without case distinction.

values.label: Other
values.note: Plays no part in sentence boundaries.

values.label: SContinue
values.note: Continues the sentence despite following a terminator, such as a comma.

values.label: STerm
values.note: Unambiguous sentence terminator, such as the question mark.

values.label: Upper
values.note: Uppercase letter.

props.name: NFC_Quick_Check
props.gloss: NFC_Quick_Check - whether the codepoint is already in Normalization Form C.
props.note: A value of No means normalising the text will replace this codepoint with something else. Anything that survives a round trip through other software unchanged must be Yes here.

values.label: No
values.note: Not in NFC; normalisation will replace it.

values.label: Yes
values.note: Already in NFC; normalisation leaves it alone.

props.name: NFD_Quick_Check
props.gloss: NFD_Quick_Check - whether the codepoint is already in Normalization Form D, the fully decomposed form.

values.label: No
values.note: Will decompose into other codepoints.

values.label: Yes
values.note: Already decomposed.

props.name: NFKC_Quick_Check
props.gloss: NFKC_Quick_Check - whether the codepoint survives compatibility normalisation to form KC.
props.note: The most consequential of the four for glyph hunting. A No here means the character is a compatibility variant that NFKC will fold away into a plainer one - which is exactly what happens to fullwidth forms, circled letters and most styled alphanumerics. 628 cells on this page are No. If software anywhere in the chain normalises, those markers do not survive it.

values.label: No
values.note: Compatibility normalisation folds this away into another character.

values.label: Yes
values.note: Survives compatibility normalisation unchanged.

props.name: NFKD_Quick_Check
props.gloss: NFKD_Quick_Check - whether the codepoint survives compatibility decomposition to form KD.

values.label: No
values.note: Compatibility decomposition replaces this with other characters.

values.label: Yes
values.note: Survives compatibility decomposition unchanged.

props.gloss: One of 0-9, A-F, a-f.

props.gloss: Counts as a letter for general text processing, including many letter-like symbols.

props.name: Bidi_Control

props.name: Case_Ignorable

props.name: Cased
props.gloss: Has a case distinction.

props.name: Changes_When_Casefolded
props.gloss: Case folding alters this codepoint.

props.name: Changes_When_Casemapped
props.gloss: Any of the case mappings alters this codepoint.

props.name: Changes_When_Lowercased
props.gloss: Lowercasing alters this codepoint.

props.name: Changes_When_NFKC_Casefolded
props.gloss: The combination of compatibility normalisation and case folding alters this codepoint. A broad marker of 'this character is a variant of a plainer one'.

props.name: Changes_When_Titlecased
props.gloss: Titlecasing alters this codepoint.

props.name: Changes_When_Uppercased
props.gloss: Uppercasing alters this codepoint.

props.name: Dash
props.gloss: A dash or hyphen of some kind, by shape and function rather than by category alone.

props.name: Default_Ignorable_Code_Point
props.gloss: Should be rendered as nothing at all if the renderer does not support it, rather than as a missing-glyph box. No cell on this page carries it, which follows from the inventory being built of things that draw.
props.inert: no cell on this page carries it

props.name: Deprecated
props.gloss: Its use is discouraged by the standard. It will not be removed, but nothing new should rely on it.

props.name: Diacritic
props.gloss: Modifies the letter it applies to, whether combining or free-standing.

props.name: Emoji
props.gloss: May be presented as emoji. Not the same as being drawn in colour by default - see Emoji_Presentation. Worth holding the tension in mind: emoji are among the most reliably *present* characters in Unicode, which by a pure coverage test makes them excellent, and among the worst candidates for carrying encoding, because they are semantically loud and already common in the content being marked up.

props.name: Emoji_Component
props.gloss: A piece that only appears inside a larger emoji sequence, such as a skin tone or a tag character.

props.name: Emoji_Modifier
props.gloss: A skin-tone modifier.
props.inert: no cell on this page carries it

props.name: Emoji_Modifier_Base
props.gloss: Can take a skin-tone modifier.

props.name: Emoji_Presentation
props.gloss: Drawn as a colour emoji by default, with no variation selector needed. The sharpest rendering hazard on this page: a colour emoji font will claim these characters, so their advance, colour and often their shape come from a font you did not choose. 91 cells here carry it. The distinction that resolves the apparent paradox - these render very consistently in one sense and not at all in another - is that coverage and metrics are consistent while the drawing is not: the same codepoint is a different picture on Apple, Google and Microsoft platforms. Consistent presence is not consistent appearance.

props.name: Expands_On_NFC
props.gloss: Normalising to form C makes this codepoint longer than it was.

props.name: Expands_On_NFD
props.gloss: Decomposing this codepoint yields more than one character.

props.name: Expands_On_NFKC
props.gloss: Compatibility normalisation to form C expands this codepoint.

props.name: Expands_On_NFKD
props.gloss: Compatibility decomposition expands this codepoint.

props.name: Extended_Pictographic
props.gloss: Pictographic in the sense the segmentation algorithms use - a superset of Emoji that includes many symbols never treated as emoji. 550 cells here carry it, so dropping the emoji blocks from the inventory did not remove pictographs from the page.

props.name: Extender
props.gloss: Extends the value of the character before it, such as a length mark.

props.name: Full_Composition_Exclusion
props.gloss: Excluded from recomposition, so decomposing and recomposing does not give back the original.

props.name: Grapheme_Base

props.name: Bidi_Mirrored
props.gloss: The glyph should be mirrored when drawn in right-to-left context. Note this is not the same as having a mirrored partner: 542 cells here are mirrored, but only 416 have another codepoint listed as their mirror in BidiMirroring.txt - the rest are expected to be flipped by the renderer with no separate character to flip to.

excluded.heading: Script text writing
excluded.why: Four clusters of one kind: Indic syllable structure, Arabic and Syriac cursive joining, Hangul composition, and the CJK radical-to-ideograph mapping. Each is machinery for writing running text in a script, so its values describe a role inside that script rather than anything about the character - which is the one exclusion this project holds to. Every one of them has a value for every codepoint, so being total says nothing; what matters is what the value is a statement about.

excluded.heading: String-valued
excluded.why: The value is another string or codepoint rather than a class, so there is no finite set to choose from. Bidi_Mirroring_Glyph is the exception: it is excluded as a filter but shown in the info box, and Bidi_Mirrored is offered instead.
